A scan of your local network shows this device’s MAC address to the devices on that network, and no app can hide it. Scans of addresses outside your network, on the internet, do not carry it. Make sure the address is a random one: in Wi-Fi settings, open the network and set Privacy to “Use randomized MAC”. For a new address on every connection, turn on “Wi-Fi non-persistent MAC randomization” in Developer options.

When a scan has ended, the report button at the top right saves the results in the app or exports them as text, CSV, or JSON.
The shield button opens your authorized ranges. Scans outside them, and outside your own network, ask you to confirm first.
A toolkit for looking at networks you own or manage. It has no ads, no tracking, and sends nothing anywhere unless you start a scan or action.
The %1$s at the top lets you arrange the dashboard. Tools marked “Soon” are not built yet.
To go back, tap the page title or use the system back gesture. Tap this title, or anywhere outside, to close windows like this one.
More choices, including any accent color, are in Settings.
Finds the devices on a network. Type an address, a range, or a network such as 192.168.1.0/24, or use the buttons in the field to fill in your Wi-Fi network or hotspot.
Tap a device to see its details and scan its ports. Your own device is listed first, marked “me”. The “?” next to the mode tells you exactly what a scan sends.
Checks which ports are open on one device, over TCP or UDP. The %1$s button in the field fills in this device’s own address, to see what it exposes.
About 100 ports with a well-known use.
Results show each open port with the service that usually runs there. That name is a guess from the port number.
Keeps the scan results you saved from the other tools.
Open a report to give it your own title and notes, export it, or delete it. The plus button imports a report that was exported as JSON. Hold a value to copy it.
Saved reports are encrypted with a key that never leaves this device, and they are not backed up. Exported files are not encrypted.
Each screen explains itself the first time you open it. The info button at the top of a screen shows it again.
Separate ports with commas, and write ranges with a dash: 22, 80, 8000-8010. Ports are numbered 1 to 65535.
Well-known ports, used by standard services such as web, mail, and SSH.
Registered ports, used by applications such as databases, games, and media servers.
Dynamic ports, handed out for short-lived connections. Rarely worth scanning.
The usual service for each port. Any program can listen on any port.
Every address in the target is probed. A device is listed as soon as one probe gets any answer from it.
The custom options are not valid yet. Open Scan Options to fix them.
Sends one ICMP echo request (type 8) with 8 bytes of data and waits for the echo reply (type 0). Many phones and firewalls ignore pings.

Opens a full TCP connection to each port (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and closes it at once. No data is sent. A completed connection means the port is open. A reset (RST) means the port is closed, which still proves the device is there. No reply means filtered or absent.

Sends one datagram to each port, shaped as a real request for the usual service: a DNS query to 53, an NTP request to 123, a NetBIOS status query to 137, an SSDP search to 1900, an mDNS query to 5353, and an empty datagram elsewhere. An answer means open. An ICMP “port unreachable” means closed. Silence proves nothing.

resources.string: Names are not looked up in this mode.
A device that ignores every probe stays invisible. SYN (half-open) scans and reading the ARP table need root, so they are not used.
For each device found, the scan asks three sources for a name and takes the first answer.
A reverse lookup (PTR record) through the DNS servers your network gave this device. That is usually your router, which often knows the names of its own devices.
A reverse lookup (PTR record) sent directly to %1$s. A public server does not know the devices on a private network.
A direct question to the device on UDP port 5353. Apple devices, Linux machines, printers, and many smart devices answer.
A status query to the device on UDP port 137. Windows and file servers answer, and may include their MAC address.
Whichever DNS server is asked learns which addresses you looked up. Choose a public server only for public addresses.
Checked every few seconds while this screen is open, by reading this device’s own network settings. Nothing is sent.

A Wi-Fi network without internet that devices can join to reach this device. Android picks the name and password. It stops when you stop it or close the app. Some devices drop their own Wi-Fi connection while it runs.

Point the other device\u2019s camera at the code, or scan it from its Wi-Fi settings. It holds the network name and password.

Android does not let apps list the devices on a hotspot, see their traffic, or block them. Finding them works with a scan of the hotspot network. Control over them needs a rooted phone.
Shows whether this device’s hotspot is on and which network it uses, and lets you scan the devices that joined it.
Turn on the normal hotspot, which shares your internet, in system settings. Or start a local-only hotspot from here: no internet, but enough for devices to reach this device.
